authors: Avramov, D.; Cheng, S.; Metzker, L.
title: Machine Learning vs. Economic Restrictions: Evidence from Stock Return Predictability
rq: Do deep-learning return signals survive economic restrictions such as excluding microcaps, distressed firms and high-volatility episodes, and trading costs?
data: US equities; ML models from the recent literature (neural networks, conditional autoencoder, IPCA, adversarial SDF) [verify full list]
universe: US common stocks, with subsamples excluding microcaps and distressed firms
features: Firm characteristics as in the replicated ML models
portfolio: Long-short and tangency portfolios implied by the models
benchmark: Unrestricted ML portfolios versus restricted universes
tcost: Reasonable trading costs applied; performance deteriorates because of high turnover and extreme positions
turnover: High; identified as the main source of cost drag
risk: Universe restrictions act as economic filters
result: ML profitability comes from difficult-to-arbitrage stocks and high limits-to-arbitrage states; excluding microcaps, distressed stocks or high-volatility episodes considerably attenuates it; costs erode it further.
contribution: Showed that headline ML alpha is concentrated where it is least implementable.
limitation: Diagnoses the problem; does not propose a combination method that is implementable by design.
not_solved: How to build ML signal combinations whose value survives restrictions and costs.
extension: Use its restrictions as the default universe and report results both with and without them [inference].

authors: Azevedo, V.; Hoegner, C.; Velikov, M.
title: The Expected Returns on Machine-Learning Strategies
rq: What are the expected returns of ML anomaly-combination strategies after costs, post-publication decay and the modern high-liquidity era?
ml: Range from simple to sophisticated ML, including LSTM
result: Sophisticated ML strategies earn net out-of-sample returns up to 1.42% per month; an LSTM combination has a six-factor generalized net alpha of 1.20% (t = 3.46).
contribution: Most direct evidence that some ML combinations remain profitable after costs and decay.
limitation: Cost handling is ex post (evaluation), not inside learning [inference].
extension: Replicate as a benchmark column in the factorial design [inference].

authors: Blitz, D.; Hanauer, M.X.; Hoogteijling, T.; Howard, C.
title: The Term Structure of Machine Learning Alpha
rq: Does ML alpha survive costs, and does training on longer prediction horizons help?
portfolio: Long-short portfolios with efficient trading rules
result: Common ML models have high full-sample gross alphas but net performance near zero after 2004; training on longer horizons (3, 6, 12 months) and efficient trading rules yields significantly positive net returns.
contribution: Showed horizon choice is a first-order lever for net ML alpha.
limitation: Horizon is fixed per model, not adapted to states or signals.
extension: Let horizon/decay enter the combination explicitly [inference].

authors: Bailey, D.H.; Lopez de Prado, M.
title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality
rq: How to correct Sharpe ratios for multiple testing and non-normality?
result: DSR corrects for selection bias under multiple testing and non-normal returns.
contribution: Standard correction for trial-count inflation.
limitation: Requires honest trial counts and correlation among trials.
extension: Log every configuration to compute DSR [inference].

authors: Collin-Dufresne, P.; Daniel, K.; Saglam, M.
title: Liquidity Regimes and Optimal Dynamic Asset Allocation
rq: How should a costly trader allocate when expected returns, covariances and trading costs follow a regime-switching model?
portfolio: Aim portfolio = weighted average of conditional MV portfolios across future states
turnover: Trading speed higher in persistent, riskier and more liquid states
result: Trading speed should vary with the regime; it can be optimal to overweight low-Sharpe assets that stay liquid in crises.
contribution: Theoretical case for state-dependent combination and trading speed under costs.
limitation: Regimes and parameters assumed known; low-dimensional.
not_solved: Empirical, high-dimensional, learned version for stock-level signals.
extension: Test its predictions (state-dependent trading speed) in an ML signal-combination setting [inference].

authors: Chen, M.; Hanauer, M.X.; Kalsbach, T.
title: Design Choices, Machine Learning, and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
rq: How much do researcher design choices change ML-based return-prediction portfolios?
features: Anomaly characteristics; with/without compression; pre-publication-only variants
ml: Multiple ML models across 1,056 design combinations
result: Seven design choices (model, target, target transformation, pre-publication inputs, feature compression, rolling vs expanding window, microcaps) generate monthly top-minus-bottom returns from 0.13% to 1.98%; the non-standard error exceeds the standard error by 59%.
contribution: Quantified non-standard errors in ML asset-pricing research.
limitation: Documents dispersion; not a combination method.
not_solved: Which choices create net-of-cost value and why.
extension: Adopt multiverse reporting for our design [inference].

title: Zeroing In on the Expected Returns of Anomalies
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 58(3):968-1004
rq: What is the expected return of anomaly strategies net of spreads, post-publication decay and modern trading technology?
tcost: Effective bid-ask spreads (high- and low-frequency estimates)
result: Net of these effects, the average anomaly earns about 4 bps per month; cost mitigation works pre-publication but net returns are tiny afterward.
contribution: Calibrates realistic expectations for signal-level alpha.
gap: Signal-level alpha is small after costs
extension: Use its spread data and horizon to set the cost baseline [inference].

title: Open Source Cross-Sectional Asset Pricing
rq: Can the cross-sectional predictor literature be reproduced with open code and data?
data: 319 characteristics in the paper; website provides 209 firm-level signals (212 incl. 3 CRSP-based) through Dec 2024
result: 98% of clearly significant predictors reproduce with t > 1.96; slope of reproduced on original t-stats is 0.88 with R2 of 82%.
contribution: Open signal library usable as the backbone of a signal-combination study.
extension: Primary open signal source [inference].

authors: DeMiguel, V.; Martin-Utrera, A.; Nogales, F.J.; Uppal, R.
title: A Transaction-Cost Perspective on the Multitude of Firm Characteristics
rq: How do transaction costs change the number of characteristics that matter jointly for an investor's optimal portfolio?
data: US equities with a large set of firm characteristics [verify count and dates]
ml: Parametric portfolio policy (linear in characteristics) with regularisation
signal: Characteristic weights estimated by maximising investor utility net of costs
portfolio: Parametric portfolio policy with transaction costs
benchmark: Policies ignoring costs; subsets of characteristics
metrics: Significance of characteristics; out-of-sample utility / Sharpe net of costs
result: Transaction costs increase the number of jointly significant characteristics from 6 to 15, because trades implied by different characteristics partly cancel out (netting).
contribution: Showed that combining many signals is valuable precisely because of trade netting under costs.
not_solved: Nonlinear and state-dependent combinations under costs.
extension: Measure netting benefits explicitly for nonlinear and conditional combinations [inference].

authors: DeMiguel, V.; Martin-Utrera, A.; Uppal, R.
title: A Multifactor Perspective on Volatility-Managed Portfolios
rq: Can conditioning factor weights on volatility add value out of sample and net of costs in a multifactor setting?
data: US factor portfolios; replication package on Mendeley Data
benchmark: Unconditional multifactor and single-factor volatility-managed portfolios
result: Single-factor volatility management does not survive costs, but a conditional multifactor portfolio outperforms its unconditional counterpart out of sample and net of costs; factor risk prices generally fall with market volatility.
contribution: Evidence that state-conditional combination can survive costs when done jointly across factors.
limitation: Low-dimensional factor set; one conditioning variable family.
extension: Generalise conditioning to many states and signals at stock level [inference].

authors: Gu, S.; Kelly, B.; Xiu, D.
title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning
rq: Which machine-learning methods best measure stock-level risk premia, and where do their gains come from?
universe: All US common stocks (roughly 30,000 over the sample) [verify exact filters]
features: 94 firm characteristics, 74 industry dummies, 8 aggregate macro predictors and characteristic x macro interactions (920 covariates) [verify counts in full text]
ml: OLS, OLS-3, PLS, PCR, elastic net, generalized linear model with group lasso, random forest, gradient-boosted trees, neural networks with 1-5 hidden layers
signal: Implicit: one pooled panel model maps all characteristics to next-month excess return
portfolio: Decile sorts on predicted returns (equal- and value-weighted long-short); market-timing exercise
benchmark: OLS with all covariates; OLS-3 (size, book-to-market, momentum)
metrics: Out-of-sample R2, Diebold-Mariano tests, variable importance, decile-spread returns and Sharpe ratios
period: Expanding training window with separate validation; out-of-sample test 1987-2016 [verify split]
tcost: Not modelled in the headline portfolio results [inference from design; verify appendix]
result: Trees and neural networks perform best; gains come from nonlinear predictor interactions; price trends, liquidity and volatility are the dominant predictors.
contribution: Set the standard comparative design for ML in cross-sectional return prediction.
limitation: Gross-of-cost sort portfolios; predictions evaluated by statistical loss, not the investor objective; static mapping over time except via macro interactions.
not_solved: Whether the predictive gains survive trading costs, implementable constraints and realistic capacity.
extension: Re-run the same model classes inside one cost-aware optimizer and attribute the net gain to nonlinearity, conditioning and objective [inference].

title: Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs
rq: What is the optimal dynamic portfolio when returns are predictable by signals with different decay speeds and trading is costly?
features: Return-predicting signals with different mean-reversion speeds
signal: Signals weighted by their persistence: slower signals get more weight in the aim portfolio
portfolio: Closed-form: trade partially toward an aim portfolio that is itself a weighted average of current and expected future Markowitz portfolios
result: Two principles: aim in front of the target and trade partially toward it.
contribution: Theory of how signal decay and costs jointly determine the combination and trading speed.
limitation: Linear signals, known dynamics, quadratic costs.
not_solved: Learning signal decay and nonlinear signal interactions from data.
extension: Estimate signal-specific decay with ML and embed in the aim portfolio [inference].

authors: Jensen, T.I.; Kelly, B.; Malamud, S.; Pedersen, L.H.
title: Machine Learning and the Implementable Efficient Frontier
rq: How should ML be used so that portfolios deliver the best risk-return trade-off net of trading costs?
data: JKP global characteristics dataset (US monthly characteristics, daily and monthly returns); WRDS access required (code README)
freq: Monthly characteristics; daily returns for risk estimation
features: JKP firm characteristics (about 150, clustered into 13 themes)
ml: Ridge-type regressions on random Fourier features; separate models for returns at horizons t+1..t+12 (code README)
signal: Learned jointly with the portfolio objective in Portfolio-ML; prediction-first in Markowitz-ML / Static-ML
portfolio: Trading-cost-aware optimisation; methods compared: Portfolio-ML, Static-ML, Static-ML*, Markowitz-ML, portfolio sorts
benchmark: Markowitz-ML, portfolio sort, 1/N, market [verify full list]
metrics: Implementable efficient frontier (net return per unit of risk), net Sharpe ratio, utility, economic feature importance
tcost: Explicit trading-cost model entering the optimisation (price impact increasing in trade size relative to liquidity) [verify calibration]
turnover: Controlled endogenously through the cost-aware objective
risk: Covariance estimate inside the mean-variance utility
result: After costs, Markowitz-ML and sorts have downward-bending frontiers; Static-ML earns positive net Sharpe but negative utility unless tuned; Portfolio-ML, which learns weights under an economic objective, works best out of sample.
contribution: Moved ML evaluation from gross prediction to the implementable frontier; introduced economic feature importance.
limitation: [inference] The paper's focus is the cost-aware objective; explicit state- or regime-dependence of signal weights and forecast uncertainty are not its central questions (verify in full text).
not_solved: [inference] How much of the net gain comes from nonlinearity versus conditioning versus the objective; whether conditioning on market states adds value once costs are internalised.
gap: Closest prior art for any cost-aware ML combination claim
extension: Use Portfolio-ML as the strongest benchmark and nest it inside a factorial decomposition [inference].

authors: Jensen, T.I.; Kelly, B.; Pedersen, L.H.
title: Is There a Replication Crisis in Finance?
rq: Do published factors replicate, and how should multiple testing be handled?
data: 153 factors, 93 countries (jkpfactors.com; CC BY-NC 4.0; updated through Dec 2025)
ml: Bayesian hierarchical model of factor alphas
result: Most factors replicate, cluster into 13 themes (most in the tangency portfolio), work out of sample across 93 countries, and evidence is strengthened by the number of factors.
contribution: Global, documented signal dataset and a Bayesian view of the factor zoo.
extension: Theme-level attribution and international robustness [inference].

title: The Cross-section of Expected Stock Returns
rq: How well do Fama-MacBeth combinations of many characteristics predict returns out of sample?
universe: All stocks, excluding tiny stocks, large stocks
ml: Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions with rolling slope averages
signal: Linear combination with historically averaged slopes
result: Fitted expected returns from rolling FM slopes have strong out-of-sample predictive power.
contribution: The canonical simple linear combination baseline.
extension: Mandatory baseline in our benchmark set [inference].

authors: Liao, Y.; Ma, X.; Neuhierl, A.; Schilling, L.
title: The Uncertainty of Machine Learning Predictions in Asset Pricing
rq: How uncertain are neural-network expected-return forecasts, and does accounting for it improve portfolios?
ml: Neural networks; closed-form and bootstrap standard errors
result: NN return forecasts share the asymptotic distribution of classic nonparametric estimators, giving closed-form standard errors; using the intervals improves out-of-sample performance.
contribution: Formal inference for ML expected returns and its portfolio use.
limitation: Working paper; cost interaction not central [inference].
not_solved: Interaction of uncertainty with trading costs and state dependence.
extension: Use as the uncertainty cell and closest prior art for Concept 3 [inference].

title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs
rq: Which anomalies survive trading costs and which mitigation techniques work?
data: US anomalies with effective spread estimates
turnover: Taxonomy by turnover (<50% per month tends to survive)
result: Buy/hold spreads are the most effective mitigation; most anomalies with under 50% monthly turnover earn significant net spreads, few with higher turnover do; size, value and profitability strategies have the most capacity.
contribution: Standard reference for anomaly trading costs and mitigation.
extension: Buy/hold spread as a strong simple benchmark [inference].

authors: Neuhierl, A.; Randl, O.; Reschenhofer, C.; Zechner, J.
title: Timing the Factor Zoo
rq: Can the returns of hundreds of equity factors be timed with a high-dimensional set of predictors?
data: 300+ equity risk factors and a high-dimensional predictor set
features: Factor-specific and aggregate predictors (past factor returns, volatility, valuation, macro, etc.)
ml: Partial least squares and other dimension-reduction/shrinkage methods
result: Almost all factor groups can be timed, most for profitability and value; past factor returns and volatility are the best single predictors but PLS aggregation dominates; timing raises the multifactor portfolio return by about 20%.
contribution: Most comprehensive evidence that factor (signal) efficacy is predictable over time.
limitation: Operates at the factor-portfolio level; stock-level netting and implementable costs are not the focus [inference].
not_solved: Whether factor-timing information survives when combined at the stock level inside a cost-aware optimizer [inference].
extension: Feed timing predictors as state variables into stock-level combination [inference].

authors: Simon, F.; Weibels, S.; Zimmermann, T.
title: Deep Parametric Portfolio Policies
venue: Management Science (2026; Crossref record) - earlier CFR Working Paper 23-01 / SSRN 4150292
rq: Do neural-network parametric portfolio policies beat linear policies?
ml: Feed-forward neural networks mapping characteristics to weight tilts
portfolio: Deep parametric portfolio policy with weight/leverage constraints
tcost: Incorporated; results robust after costs [verify whether costs enter training]
result: Network-based policies achieve 75-276 bps higher monthly certainty-equivalent returns than a comparable linear policy, robust to costs and short-sale restrictions.
contribution: Nonlinear generalisation of PPP under an economic objective.
limitation: Static mapping; state dependence and uncertainty not central [inference].
extension: Benchmark column; nonlinear-objective cell [inference].

title: Lest We Forget: Learn from Out-of-Sample Forecast Errors When Optimizing Portfolios
rq: Are errors in historical forecasts of optimisation inputs predictable, and can learning from them improve portfolios?
data: Portfolio datasets; replication data on Harvard Dataverse
metrics: Out-of-sample Sharpe, realised vs expected performance
result: Forecast errors have predictable patterns; learning from them yields portfolios whose performance meets expectations.
contribution: Links forecast-error learning to optimiser robustness.
extension: Calibrate ML alpha scale by realised forecast errors [inference].

authors: Brandt, M.W.; Santa-Clara, P.; Valkanov, R.
title: Parametric Portfolio Policies: Exploiting Characteristics in the Cross-Section of Equity Returns
rq: Can portfolio weights be modelled directly as a function of stock characteristics instead of estimating return distributions?
ml: Parametric (linear) weight function estimated by maximising average utility
signal: Weights tilt linearly on standardized characteristics
result: Direct weight modelling scales to large cross-sections and delivers economically large gains.
contribution: Foundation of learning portfolio weights under an economic objective.
not_solved: Nonlinearity, many signals, costs, state dependence.
extension: Nonlinear/conditional PPP generalisations (see DMNU2020, SWZ2023, JKMP2026).

authors: Capponi, A.; Huang, C.; Sidaoui, J.A.; Wang, K.; Zou, J.
title: The Nonstationarity-Complexity Tradeoff in Return Prediction
rq: How should model complexity and training-window length be chosen jointly in non-stationary markets?
data: US equity industry portfolios, three decades
ml: Adaptive joint selection of complexity and window with guarantees
result: Adaptive selection improves out-of-sample R2 on industry portfolios by 14% relative to fixed-window and regime-switching benchmarks, with large gains in recessions.
contribution: Formalises the window/complexity trade-off.
limitation: Statistical loss; portfolio-level costs not studied [inference].
extension: Treat window choice as a design factor [inference].

authors: Chen, L.; Pelger, M.; Zhu, J.
title: Deep Learning in Asset Pricing
rq: Can deep networks estimate a flexible, time-varying SDF for individual stocks using no-arbitrage as the criterion?
data: US stocks with firm characteristics and many macroeconomic time series
features: Firm characteristics; macro states extracted from many macro series [verify counts]
ml: Adversarial (GAN-style) networks; recurrent networks for macro states
benchmark: Linear and other ML SDF models
metrics: SDF Sharpe, explained variation, pricing errors
result: No-arbitrage criterion, adversarial test assets and macro states improve SDF estimation.
contribution: State-dependent deep SDF.
limitation: Implementability; ACM2023 show such portfolios suffer under restrictions.
extension: Macro-state extraction ideas for state variables [inference].

authors: Frazzini, A.; Israel, R.; Moskowitz, T.J.
title: Trading Costs
rq: What are actual institutional trading costs across trade types, stock characteristics, sizes, time and exchanges?
data: $1.7 trillion of live trade execution data from a large institutional manager, 21 developed markets, 19 years
result: Actual trading costs are an order of magnitude smaller than previous studies suggest.
contribution: Best available calibration anchor for institutional price impact.
limitation: Single manager's execution; not public data.
extension: Use as calibration range; run cost-multiplier sensitivity [inference].

authors: Haddad, V.; Kozak, S.; Santosh, S.
title: Factor Timing
rq: Are the dominant components of anomaly returns predictable, and what does that imply for the SDF?
result: Market-neutral factors are strongly and robustly predictable; timing substantially improves performance relative to static factor investing.
contribution: Shows the optimal timing portfolio equals the SDF; disciplined low-dimensional timing.
extension: Use PC-valuation predictors as state variables [inference].

authors: Lalwani, V.; Meshram, V.; Jindal, V.
title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning: The Role of Research Design Choices
rq: How do eight research design choices, including training window, data filters and portfolio construction, affect ML strategy profits?
result: Non-standard errors are up to five times the standard errors; about one-third of portfolios earn significant returns after costs.
contribution: Extends non-standard-error evidence to portfolio construction choices.
extension: Multiverse robustness appendix [inference].

title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
rq: What happens to anomaly returns out of sample and after publication?
result: Portfolio returns are 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower post-publication.
contribution: Documented signal decay after publication.
extension: Publication-date-aware signal availability and decay features [inference].

title: In Good and in Bad Times? The Relation between Anomaly Returns and Market States
rq: Do anomalies perform differently in good versus bad market states?
result: Anomalies perform better in unfavourable market states, driven mostly by the short side (reported magnitudes differ between SSRN and journal versions; verify).
contribution: Global evidence of state-dependent anomaly efficacy.
extension: Motivates state-conditional signal weights [inference].

authors: Rapach, D.E.; Strauss, J.K.; Zhou, G.
title: Out-of-Sample Equity Premium Prediction: Combination Forecasts and Links to the Real Economy
rq: Can combining individual predictive-regression forecasts beat the historical average out of sample?
data: US equity premium with Welch-Goyal predictors
result: Combination forecasts deliver consistent out-of-sample gains because model uncertainty and instability impair individual models.
contribution: Classic evidence that simple combination dominates under instability.
extension: Simple averaging as a benchmark for dynamic weights [inference].

title: Does It Pay to Follow Anomalies Research? Machine Learning Approach with International Evidence
rq: Do ML aggregations of published anomalies earn out-of-sample returns globally?
ml: ML aggregation into a single mispricing signal
result: ML aggregation of all anomalies is profitable around the globe and survives in a liquid universe; non-US past performance does not help pick US winners.
contribution: International out-of-sample evidence for ML anomaly aggregation.
limitation: Cost treatment via universe rather than optimiser.
extension: International robustness template [inference].

title: Meta-Learning for Return Prediction in Shifting Market Regimes
rq: Can a meta-learned prior-fitted network adapt return prediction to regime shifts?
result: Superior performance relative to ML benchmarks, especially in turbulent periods.
contribution: Brings meta-learning / in-context learning to regime-shifting return prediction.
extension: Adaptive cell in robustness [inference].

title: Augmented Investment Management: A systematic framework for designing alpha models
venue: Industry white paper (BlackRock, Nov 2025; for professional investors)
rq: How can ML automate the combination of a large signal library into alpha forecasts for a portfolio optimizer?
data: Proprietary signal library (~1,200 stock-selection signals by 2025 per Figure 1); 10-20 years of training data
features: Signals from financial statements, market indicators, news, analyst reports, alternative data
ml: Regularised linear models, gradient boosting ensembles, neural networks, proprietary variants; large configuration search; cross-validation
signal: Reframes signal weighting as forecasting excess returns (alpha forecasts)
portfolio: Separate high-fidelity optimizer with transaction costs, borrow costs, fund constraints; parameters tuned to maximise a metric such as IR
benchmark: Discretionary weighting (conceptually); baseline vs defensive model
tcost: Inside the performance simulator and optimizer; details not disclosed
risk: Risk model in optimizer; neutralisation of risk factors optional
result: Qualitative framework; illustrative defensive model trained on resampled negative regimes had lower drawdowns but about a 20% performance haircut; Shapley-based attribution reveals a nonlinear volatility effect.
contribution: Documents an industrial predict-then-optimize ML pipeline with regime resampling and SHAP-style attribution.
limitation: No out-of-sample statistical evidence, no cost-adjusted results, proprietary data; regime-awareness by resampling, not state-conditional weights; hyperparameter search inflates trial counts.
not_solved: Whether ML combination adds value net of costs, which component creates it, and how to adapt to signal decay (listed by the authors as ongoing research: adaptive/online learning, domain adaptation).
extension: Our design makes each AIM component a testable factor [inference].

authors: Cakici, N.; Fieberg, C.; Metko, D.; Zaremba, A.
title: Machine Learning Goes Global: Cross-Sectional Return Predictability in International Stock Markets
venue: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 155:104725
rq: How does ML return predictability vary across 46 stock markets?
ml: Repertoire of ML models and their combination
result: Predictability comes mainly from momentum, reversal, value and size; combining models is particularly effective; performance depends on firm size, recency of information, market breadth and idiosyncratic risk.
contribution: Global cross-country evidence.
extension: Out-of-US robustness [inference].

authors: Kelly, B.; Malamud, S.; Zhou, K.
title: The Virtue of Complexity in Return Prediction
rq: Can models with more parameters than observations improve out-of-sample return prediction?
data: US market return with standard predictors
result: Complex models dominate simple ones in theory and US market timing; strategies divest before recessions (14 of 15 out of sample).
contribution: Theoretical rationale for high-complexity ML in return prediction.
not_solved: Complexity vs costs in cross-sectional combination.
extension: Complexity dimension in design [inference].

authors: Arnott, R.; Harvey, C.R.; Markowitz, H.
title: A Backtesting Protocol in the Era of Machine Learning
result: Checklist-style protocol for credible ML backtests.

authors: Bailey, D.H.; Borwein, J.; Lopez de Prado, M.; Zhu, Q.J.
title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
result: CSCV estimates the probability that the in-sample best configuration underperforms out of sample.

title: FR-LUX: Friction-Aware, Regime-Conditioned Policy Optimization for Implementable Portfolio Management
result: Reinforcement-learning policy with proportional and impact costs inside the reward, inaction bands, conditioning on four volatility-liquidity regimes; evaluated on a regime x cost grid with bootstrap CIs and multiple-testing corrections; reports a flatter cost-performance slope than baselines.
limitation: Closest new prior art for the conditioning x cost interaction (gap G2); cite and differentiate (single method vs factorial attribution; small asset space vs ~150-signal cross-section).

title: A Test for Superior Predictive Ability
result: SPA test: more powerful and less sensitive to poor alternatives than the Reality Check.

authors: Harvey, C.R.; Liu, Y.; Zhu, H.

result: Multiple-testing framework for 300+ factors; new factors should clear t > 3.0.

title: Robust Performance Hypothesis Testing with the Sharpe Ratio
result: HAC and studentised circular block bootstrap tests for Sharpe-ratio differences.

title: Spurious Predictability in Financial Machine Learning
result: Adaptive specification search produces statistically significant backtests under martingale-difference nulls; proposes a falsification audit with zero-predictability reference classes, microstructure placebos and a multiplicity-adjusted inflation gap.

title: A Reality Check for Data Snooping

authors: Ardia, D.; Guidotti, E.; Kroencke, T.A.
title: Efficient Estimation of Bid-Ask Spreads from Open, High, Low, and Close Prices
result: EDGE estimator from OHLC prices; R package 'bidask'.

title: Integrating Prediction in Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization
result: Integrated prediction-optimisation (IPO) with closed forms for unconstrained MVO and differentiable QP layers otherwise; lower realised cost than predict-then-optimize.

authors: Bryzgalova, S.; Lerner, S.; Lettau, M.; Pelger, M.
title: Missing Financial Data
result: Characteristics are frequently missing, not at random; proposes cross-sectional and time-series imputation. [verify pages]

title: Conformal Predictive Portfolio Selection
result: Combines conformal prediction intervals with portfolio selection across AR, random-forest and neural-network forecasters.
limitation: Basis for uncertainty level D2 (calibrated intervals) instead of raw ensemble dispersion.

authors: Ceria, S.; Saxena, A.; Stubbs, R.A.
title: Factor Alignment Problems and Quantitative Portfolio Management
result: Misalignment between alpha model, risk model and constraints creates unintended exposures and risk underestimation.

authors: Clarke, R.; de Silva, H.; Thorley, S.

authors: Cong, L.W.; Tang, K.; Wang, J.; Zhang, Y.

result: Transformer-based RL directly optimises investor objectives; out-of-sample Sharpe above 2 and 13%+ alpha with monthly rebalancing in US equities, robust to excluding small/illiquid stocks; 'economic distillation' for interpretation.

title: Approximately Normal Tests for Equal Predictive Accuracy in Nested Models
result: Adjusted MSPE test for nested models.

result: About 200 published anomalies: median return 48 bp/month through 2005 falls to 19 bp post-2005 and to about 7 bp after liquidity/microcap restrictions; modest cost allowances eliminate it.

result: Generalised method of moments approach to missing characteristics; imputation choices affect results. [verify pages]

result: Adaptive group LASSO selects characteristics with incremental information and estimates nonlinear effects; many predictors add nothing incremental; nonlinearity matters.
